newsitem.title: THAILAND: THAIS SAY RUBBER PRODUCERS CONSIDERING SUPPLY CUTS.
newsitem.headline: THAIS SAY RUBBER PRODUCERS CONSIDERING SUPPLY CUTS.

text.p: Major rubber-producing countries are considering ways to cut back on supplies to help shore up falling prices, a senior Thai agriculture official said on Thursday.

Sucharit Promdej, an advisor to the agriculture ministry, told Reuters the idea was floated during a meeting of the Association of Rubber Producing Countries in the Thai rubber centre of Hat Yai this week.
The meeting of the Coordinating Committee on Production and Marketing Strategies lasted three days and ended on Thursday.
"If we look at the boom/bust cycle in rubber, the trend points towards the possibility that the bearish trend could continue until 1999 following the boom of 1994-1995," he said.
"We need collaborative action among member countries to tackle this problem," Sucharit said.
The committee came up with several recommendations to temporarily cut rubber supplies and prop up prices.
It suggested member countries should lobby the private sector to hold bigger commercial stocks and recommended that governments introduce tapping holidays, he said.
Sucharit said accelerating a replanting scheme was also an option. Under the scheme, old rubber trees will be cut down to limit supplies from this source.
He said such measures could be difficult to implement in Thailand, the world's biggest natural rubber producer, as the industry is dominated by small holders.
"It is almost impossible to manage supplies with small holders. These people are used to tapping without looking at the market and that leads to a glut," he said.

"The government needs to create awareness that if they don't manage their tapping, they will be hurt by low prices. The government will also have to help them find other sources of income before limiting tapping," he said.
Sucharit said industry officials from other major producers such as Malaysia and Indonesia will present the ideas arising at the meeting to their respective governments.
Thailand will also try to boost local consumption of rubber, he said.

The country aims to increase local consumption to 240,000 tonnes, or more than 10 percent of local supply, by the year 2000. Domestic rubber consumption here presently accounts for only seven to eight percent of national production.
Thailand forecasts that it's natural rubber output will reach 2.03 million tonnes in 1998, 2.13 million tonnes in 1999 and 2.24 million tonnes in 2000.
